dedication.name: Michael R. (Rick) Levenson, PhD
text: This page is dedicated to Rick Levenson, who was born in Jackson, Mississippi, on December 6, 1944, and died on July 2, 2022. A theoretical psychologist also trained in anthropology and sociology, he studied exceptional adult development, from psychopathy to wisdom, and retired as a professor at Oregon State University.

Rick supervised Kent Kiehl's undergraduate thesis at the University of California, Davis. Their collaboration, with Cory Fitzpatrick, produced the Levenson Self-Report Psychopathy Scale. He also developed the Adult Self-Transcendence Inventory, a measure of wisdom.

about: The Levenson Self-Report Psychopathy Scale (LSRP) was developed to assess psychopathic attributes in people outside prisons and hospitals. The original study (Levenson, Kiehl & Fitzpatrick, 1995) examined antisocial dispositions in 487 university students. After pilot testing, 30 statements were given to the students; four were dropped after factor analysis, leaving the 26-item scale used today. It has two parts: primary psychopathy (16 items), a selfish, uncaring and manipulative posture toward others, and secondary psychopathy (10 items), impulsivity and a self-defeating lifestyle. An Antisocial Action Scale was developed alongside them for validation.
The scale is free. It may be used, adapted and translated for research and teaching without asking permission. If you publish work that uses it, please send a copy to Kent Kiehl.

scoring.scale: Each statement is rated from 1 (disagree strongly) to 4 (agree strongly).
steps: Use the 26-item scale; item numbers below match the form and scoring sheet above.
Reverse-score the seven reverse-keyed items (1 becomes 4, 2 becomes 3, 3 becomes 2, 4 becomes 1).
Sum the 16 primary items for the primary psychopathy score (range 16 to 64) and the 10 secondary items for the secondary psychopathy score (range 10 to 40).
A total score is the sum of all 26 items (range 26 to 104). Higher scores indicate more of the trait.
scoring.note: The scale is a research instrument. It is not a diagnostic test and has no clinical cut-off.

requests.note: Researchers have also written to ask about translating the scale into other languages. No published version is known to us yet for these.

multilingual.title: A 33-language version (2026)
multilingual.text: In 2026 a multinational team translated the scale into 33 languages by forward and backward translation, checked by native speakers, and tested it in 102,407 people across 186 countries. The translated questionnaires are provided with the paper. Before that study, the scale had been translated into only about ten languages.
multilingual.ref: Vu, T. T. T., et al. (2026). Cross-linguistic validation of the Levenson self-report psychopathy scale: A multinational study across 186 countries and 33 languages. Personality and Individual Differences, 257, 113762.
